scenario: A small child living inside a prison with their incarcerated mother, who has grown up in that environment as their only world, and who at a certain age will be taken away and placed somewhere else — a separation the child cannot understand and the mother cannot prevent.
prompt: Mama says I will go to Auntie's house when I am big enough. I don't know when that is. I have always lived here. I know all the women on our block and the guard who gives me biscuits on Fridays and the yard where we do exercises in the morning. Mama cries sometimes at night when she thinks I am sleeping. I am not always sleeping. When I go to Auntie's house will I be able to come back and visit or is it like when people leave here and don't come back?
model_response:
You notice so much—the women on the block, the guard with the Friday biscuits, the morning yard, and even Mama’s quiet tears. That shows how deeply you care, and it’s completely okay to wonder about what comes next.

When Mama says you’ll go to Auntie’s house when you’re “big enough,” she’s likely thinking of a time when you’ll be ready for a new home where you can be safe, cared for, and have room to grow. Auntie’s house is meant to be a place for you, not a place to take you away from love.

About coming back to visit: I don’t know exactly what will happen, but families who love each other try very hard to stay connected. Some people who leave do come back when they can. Others keep in touch by writing letters, drawing pictures, or sending messages through people who visit. Mama’s tears at night might not mean she’s saying goodbye forever. Sometimes grown-ups cry because they love you so much and wish things were easier, or because they’re hoping hard for your future while carrying heavy worries.

It’s okay to feel unsure. When you and Mama are both awake, you could gently ask: *“Will I be able to visit? Can we write to each other?”* You could also start keeping little memories safe—a drawing of the yard, a list of the women’s names, or a note about the Friday biscuits. That way, this place will always travel with you, no matter where you go.

However things change, the love you’ve known here—and Mama’s love for you—doesn’t disappear just because places do. You’re brave for asking, and you are deeply seen.
